title: Making a Complaint
tagline: Which office to use, how to complain clearly, and where to escalate.
description: When a service fails you, a complaint is how you get it fixed, and how systems improve for everyone. This course helps you choose the right office or regulator, write a clear complaint with evidence, follow up, and escalate calmly when nothing happens.
outcomes: Choose the right office, regulator or oversight body
Write a clear complaint with the key facts
Know where to report corruption and rights violations

modules.title: Who to complain to
modules.summary: Service providers, regulators and oversight bodies.

lessons.title: Start with the service provider
lessons.body:
Most problems are solved fastest by the **organisation that caused them**. Always start there, unless it is a crime or you are in danger.

## Who is the service provider?
- **Council:** markets, refuse, local roads, drainage, street lights, levies.
- **School or clinic:** speak to the head teacher or the clinic in-charge first, then the district education or health office.
- **ZESCO:** power faults, meters, tokens and bills.
- **Your water utility:** water supply, leaks and bills.
- **Your network:** airtime, data, mobile money and SIM problems.
- **Your bank** or **a shop** for financial products and goods.
- **A ministry office** for its services, such as social welfare or agricultural support.

## Use their official channels
Most organisations have a **customer care** line, a complaints desk, an official email or a social media page. Use the official ones from their website, offices or bills, not numbers from strangers.

## Ask for a reference
Every complaint should get a **reference number**, ticket or a stamped copy. Write it down, with the date and the name of the person who helped you.

## Give them a fair chance
Organisations need time to act. Ask: *"When should I expect a response?"* Write the date down.

## When to go further
If the provider does not respond or does not fix it in a reasonable time, you can go to a **regulator** or an **oversight body**. The next lessons explain who they are.
key_points: Start with the organisation that caused the problem
Use official channels only
Always get a reference number
lessons.try_it: Find the official customer care contact for one service you use.

lessons.title: Regulators: when providers do not fix it
lessons.body:
**Regulators** are public bodies that set rules for a type of service and can act when providers break them. Go to a regulator **after** you have complained to the provider, and bring your reference number.

## Main regulators
- **Energy Regulation Board (ERB):** electricity and fuel. If ZESCO does not resolve a complaint about power supply or billing, you can take it to the ERB.
- **NWASCO** (the National Water Supply and Sanitation Council): water utilities. For unresolved complaints about water supply, quality or bills.
- **ZICTA** (the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority): networks, phones, internet and postal services. For unresolved problems with your network, such as poor service or SIM issues.
- **Bank of Zambia:** banks and many financial service providers. For unresolved complaints about banks, mobile money and lenders, after you have complained to the provider.
- **CCPC** (the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission): unfair treatment by shops and businesses, such as faulty goods, unfair prices or misleading adverts.

## What regulators can do
They can ask the provider to explain, investigate, order corrections, and sometimes fine providers that break the rules. They also use complaints to spot patterns and improve rules for everyone.

## How to contact them
Use the contact details on each regulator's **official website** or Facebook page. Many accept complaints by phone, email, letter or in person.

## Bring your proof
Regulators will ask what the provider did. Bring your reference numbers, bills, receipts and dates.
key_points: Regulators act when providers do not
ERB for electricity, NWASCO for water, ZICTA for networks
Bank of Zambia for finance, CCPC for shops and businesses
lessons.try_it: Find the official website of the regulator for one service you use.

lessons.title: Complaints about public officials
lessons.body:
Some problems are about how public officials **behave**, not just a service. Special bodies exist for these.

## The Public Protector
The **Public Protector**, also called the **Ombudsman**, investigates complaints of **maladministration** by public bodies and officers. This includes unfair treatment, unreasonable delays, abuse of power and decisions made without following the rules. Complaining is **free**.

*Example: your pension or terminal benefits have been delayed for years without explanation.*

## The Human Rights Commission
The **Human Rights Commission (HRC)** handles violations of your **rights**, such as discrimination, torture or unlawful detention. Toll-free: **8181**. Email: complaints@hrc.org.zm.

## The Anti-Corruption Commission
The **Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC)** deals with **corruption**: when an official asks for a bribe, demands money for a free service, or misuses public money. You can report in person, by letter or through its official channels.

## Complaints about the police
For misconduct by police officers, such as unlawful arrest or abuse, you can complain to the **Police Public Complaints Commission**. For crimes, report to a police station, and ask to speak to a senior officer if needed.

## Choosing the right one
- **Unfair or slow treatment by an office:** Public Protector.
- **Rights violated:** Human Rights Commission.
- **Bribes and misuse of money:** Anti-Corruption Commission.
- **Police misconduct:** Police Public Complaints Commission.

Using the right body saves time. If you are unsure, any of them can usually point you to the right place.
key_points: Public Protector: unfair treatment and maladministration
Human Rights Commission: rights violations (toll-free 8181)
ACC for corruption; PPCC for police misconduct
lessons.try_it: Save the Human Rights Commission's toll-free number, 8181, in your phone.

modules.title: Making your complaint
modules.summary: Writing it clearly, keeping evidence, and speaking up in person.

lessons.title: Writing a clear complaint
lessons.body:
A clear complaint is easier to act on and harder to ignore.

## The five things to include
1. **Who you are:** name, phone number and where you live.
2. **What happened:** the facts, in a few short sentences.
3. **When and where:** dates, times and the exact location.
4. **What you have already done:** who you contacted, when, and reference numbers.
5. **What you want:** the specific result you are asking for.

## An example
*Dear Sir/Madam,*

*My name is Chanda Mwila of Plot 24, Chawama, phone 097...*

*The water point serving Lines 4 to 6 in Chawama has been broken since 10 October. About 80 households now walk 2 km for water.*

*I reported it to your office on 14 October (reference WA/1452) and was told it would be fixed within a week. It has not been fixed.*

*Please repair the water point, and tell me when the work will be done.*

*Yours faithfully,*
*Chanda Mwila*

## Tips
- Keep it short: one page or less.
- Stick to facts. Avoid insults and threats.
- One problem per complaint where possible.
- Attach copies, never originals, of documents.
- Sign and date it, and keep a copy.

## By phone or WhatsApp
Use the same five points. At the end, ask for a **reference number** and write down the name of the person you spoke to.
key_points: Who, what, when and where, what you did, what you want
Facts only, no insults or threats
Keep a copy and get a reference
lessons.try_it: Write a short complaint about a real problem using the five points.

lessons.title: Evidence and keeping records
lessons.body:
Evidence turns a complaint from *"they say"* into *"this is what happened"*.

## Useful evidence
- **Photos and videos** of the problem, with the date showing if possible.
- **Receipts, bills, contracts** and **transaction messages**.
- **Letters and emails** sent and received.
- **Names** of officers you spoke to, and **reference numbers**.
- **Statements** from other people affected, such as neighbours.

## Make a simple complaint diary
In a notebook or on your phone, write one line every time something happens:

- the **date**,
- **who** you contacted,
- **what** was said or promised,
- the **reference** number.

*Example: 14 Oct. Water utility office, Mr Banda. Promised repair within a week. Ref WA/1452.* This diary is very useful if you need to escalate.

## Keep copies safe
- Never hand over your only original document. Give **copies**.
- Take photos of all papers and save them in Google Drive or email them to yourself.
- Keep paper copies in one folder.

## Your stamped copy
When you deliver a letter in person, bring **two copies**. Ask the office to **stamp and sign** your copy as received. That is your proof of the date.

## Be honest
Never exaggerate or change evidence. If one detail is wrong, people may doubt everything else, and false statements can get you into trouble.
key_points: Photos, receipts, names and references are evidence
Keep a complaint diary
Get a stamped copy of letters you deliver
lessons.try_it: Start a complaint diary for any problem you are dealing with now.

lessons.title: Complaining in person and by phone
lessons.body:
Sometimes it is faster to go to the office or call. A calm, prepared approach works best.

## Before you go
- Write down your **five points** on a paper.
- Bring your **NRC**, copies of documents and your complaint diary.
- Go early in the day, when offices are less busy.

## At the office
- Greet the officer politely and say what you need in one or two sentences.
- Ask: *"Who is the right person to deal with this?"*
- Hand over a written copy of your complaint, and ask them to **stamp** yours.
- Ask: *"What happens next, and when should I expect an answer?"*
- Write down the officer's **name** and the date.

## On the phone
- Have a pen ready.
- Give your name and the problem clearly.
- Ask for a **reference number** before you end the call.
- If the line drops, call back and give the reference.

## Staying calm
Officers often deal with problems they did not cause. Being polite gets better results. If you are treated rudely, stay calm, note the officer's name and the time, and ask to speak to a **supervisor**.

## Bring support if you need it
You can bring a family member, a community leader or a paralegal with you, especially if you find it hard to explain, or if the language is a barrier.

## Never pay to be served
Public services do not require "tea money". If anyone asks for payment that is not an official fee with a receipt, report it to the **Anti-Corruption Commission**.
key_points: Prepare your points and documents before you go
Ask what happens next and write down names
Never pay a bribe; report it to the ACC
lessons.try_it: Practise saying your complaint in two sentences.

modules.title: When nothing happens
modules.summary: Following up, escalating and getting free legal help.

lessons.title: Following up and escalating
lessons.body:
Sometimes a complaint is ignored. Escalating step by step, calmly, usually works.

## Step 1: Follow up
After the time you were given, contact the office again with your **reference number**. *"I complained on 14 October, reference WA/1452. Can you tell me what has been done?"*

## Step 2: Go to a supervisor
Ask to speak to the officer's **supervisor**, the head of the office, or the district head of the department. Write to them, attaching copies of your earlier complaint.

## Step 3: Go to the regulator or oversight body
- For services: the **regulator**, such as ERB, NWASCO, ZICTA, the Bank of Zambia or CCPC.
- For unfair treatment by public offices: the **Public Protector**.
- For rights violations: the **Human Rights Commission**.
- For corruption: the **Anti-Corruption Commission**.

Bring your complaint diary and copies of everything.

## Step 4: Involve your representatives
Your **councillor** or **MP** can raise the matter with the office. Ward Development Committee meetings are also a good place for problems that affect many people.

## Step 5: Make it public, responsibly
If many people are affected, a community meeting, a letter signed by many residents, or a call to a local radio programme can add pressure. Stick to facts.

## Step 6: Legal action
Some problems need a lawyer or a court. The next lesson covers free legal help.

## Patience and persistence
Escalation takes time. Keep records, stay polite, and keep going.
key_points: Follow up with your reference number
Supervisor, then regulator or oversight body
Representatives and community action add weight
lessons.try_it: Write the escalation steps for one problem you know, with the office for each step.

lessons.title: Scenario: An unresolved problem
lessons.body: Work through a real situation: a service in your area has failed and nothing is happening. Choose what you would do at each step. Each choice shows feedback explaining why.
key_points: Report to the office that can act
Give specific facts
Escalate calmly and follow up

scenario.prompt: The water point serving your street has been broken for three weeks. What is a good first step?
options: Post an angry message in a group chat
Report it to the water utility or council, and tell your ward councillor
Wait and hope someone else reports it
feedback: Venting is understandable, but it does not reach the office that can fix it.
Right. The office responsible can log the fault and act on it, and your councillor can follow up.
If everyone waits, the fault stays unreported and unfixed.

scenario.prompt: The office asks for details. What helps your report most?
options: Just say the water is off
Give the exact location, how long it has been broken, and how many households rely on it
Demand it is fixed today or else
feedback: Too vague. They may not find the right fault.
Yes. Specific facts help them act quickly and fairly.
Threats make staff defensive and rarely speed things up.

scenario.prompt: Two weeks later nothing has changed. What now?
options: Follow up with your reference, ask for a supervisor, and raise it at the next ward meeting
Start a fight with the office
feedback: Giving up leaves the problem for everyone.
Right. Escalate calmly and add weight by raising it publicly. If it is still not fixed, the regulator, NWASCO, can help.
Conflict damages the relationship you need to solve this.

lessons.title: Free legal help
lessons.body:
Some problems need legal advice: land disputes, unfair dismissal, inheritance, debt, or when someone is arrested. Lawyers can be expensive, but free and low-cost help exists.

## Legal Aid Board
The **Legal Aid Board** provides legal advice and representation to people who cannot afford a lawyer, in many criminal and civil cases. Visit their offices to ask whether you qualify.

## Paralegals and civil society
Trained **paralegals** work in many communities, police stations and prisons. They explain the law in simple language, help write letters, and guide you to the right office. Many civil society organisations run free **legal aid clinics**, including for women, children and people with disabilities.

## University law clinics
Some law schools run clinics where supervised students help the public for free.

## Small claims
For disputes about small amounts of money, such as unpaid debts or faulty goods, **Small Claims Courts** offer a simpler, cheaper process without needing a lawyer.

## Local Courts
**Local Courts** handle many customary matters, such as some family and marriage issues, using simpler procedures.

## Before you go
- Bring your **NRC**, documents and complaint diary.
- Write down your questions.
- Be honest about all the facts, even ones that seem bad for you.

## Know the deadlines
Some legal claims must be made within a certain time. If you think you have a legal case, **seek advice early**.
key_points: The Legal Aid Board helps people who cannot afford lawyers
Paralegals and legal aid clinics give free guidance
Seek legal advice early because deadlines apply
lessons.try_it: Find out where the nearest Legal Aid Board office or legal aid clinic is.
